--- Page 1 ---
FunSearch and Structured SAT Search
for Weak Schur Partitions
Rebecca Vicenzi1
Pablo Christofferson2
Caleb Hartman3
Jingxuan Feng4
Suleman Khan5
Omar M. Elshinawy6
Eric Ramos7
1University of Bologna
2Carleton College
3Waynesburg University
4University of Southern California
5Rochester Institute of Technology
6University of Münster
7Stevens Institute of Technology
Abstract
The weak Schur problem asks how large an interval of consecutive integers can be parti-
tioned into a fixed number of classes with no class containing a monochromatic solution to
a + b = c with a̸ = b. We investigate whether FunSearch, an evolutionary program-search
method guided by a large language model, can discover effective construction strategies for this
classical combinatorial problem. In our adaptation, FunSearch evolves a priority function
used by a fixed greedy solver, while a separate validity check enforces the weakly sum-free
condition. This approach matches the known exact values for two, three, and four classes
and reaches WS(5) ≥195. We then explore a complementary SAT-based approach. Guided
by structural information from a 207-element construction communicated by Fred Rowley
(Rowley, 2026), our SAT search produces and verifies a distinct valid five-class partition of
{1, . . . , 207}. Thus the strongest construction obtained in this project reaches WS(5) ≥207,
eleven integers beyond the best published lower bound of 196.
The contrast between the
two approaches also exposes a limitation of our FunSearch formulation: its greedy solver
makes local, irreversible decisions, whereas SAT can enforce global structure across the whole
partition.

1
Introduction
The weak Schur problem asks how large an interval {1, . . . , N} can be while admitting a partition
into a fixed number of classes, each free of solutions to a + b = c with a̸ = b inside a single class.
Prior work has used constructive combinatorial arguments and computational search, including
SAT-based methods (Eliahou et al., 2012; Heule, 2018; Ageron et al., 2022).
FunSearch (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024) uses a large language model to evolve a short, au-
tomatically scored program that constructs a mathematical object. We apply this idea by fixing
a simple greedy constructor and evolving the priority function that decides which class to try
for each new integer. A separate validity check ensures that accepted placements preserve weak
sum-freeness.
The final FunSearch program constructs a verified five-class partition of [1, 195], establishing
WS(5) ≥195. A complementary structured SAT search constructs a verified partition of [1, 207].
The latter is the strongest result obtained in this work and exceeds by eleven the 196 lower bound
reported by Eliahou et al. (2012).
This paper presents two computational constructions with their algorithms and explicit, in-
dependently checkable certificates. The structured SAT construction establishing WS(5) ≥207
is the principal result; the FunSearch construction at 195 provides the complementary greedy
approach.
2
The Weak Schur Problem
A set of positive integers A is sum-free if it contains no solution to a + b = c, including equal
summands a = b. It is weakly sum-free if it contains no such solution with distinct summands.
Thus the weak condition is
a, b ∈A,
a < b
=⇒
a + b /∈A.
(1)
For example, {1, 2, 4, 8} is weakly sum-free but not sum-free: 1 + 1 = 2 is allowed by the weak
condition. Together with {3, 5, 6, 7}, it gives a weakly sum-free two-class partition of [1, 8].
The weak Schur number WS(k) is the largest N for which [1, N] = {1, . . . , N} can be parti-
tioned into k weakly sum-free classes. One valid partition establishes a lower bound WS(k) ≥N.
An exact value additionally requires proving that no partition of [1, N + 1] exists. The known
small values are
WS(1) = 2,
WS(2) = 8,
WS(3) = 23,
WS(4) = 66
(Eliahou et al., 2012; Heule, 2018). For five classes, Eliahou et al. (2012) exhibited a partition of
[1, 196]; subsequent template methods developed further weak Schur constructions (Ageron et al.,
2022).
Our task is to construct five lists of integers whose entries cover a long consecutive interval
exactly once, with each list weakly sum-free. These are the class lists used by our greedy con-
structor and returned by decoding the SAT output. A class label can also be called a colour; a
forbidden sum is then a monochromatic triple.
3
FunSearch
FunSearch searches over programs that construct solutions. Here, the model proposes
Python priority rules that a fixed solver uses to construct weak Schur partitions.
FunSearch improves candidate functions through repeated generation, execution and scoring
(Romera-Paredes et al., 2024).
A fixed evaluator measures each construction, and promising
programs become examples for later model proposals.
2


--- Page 3 ---
The roles in our application are as follows.
Fixed. The greedy solver, the validity check for a placement, and the evaluator that scores the
resulting construction.
Evolved. Only the function priority, which expresses which class the solver should try first.
Candidate program. An executable Python implementation of priority.
Model input. Examples of earlier candidate priority functions, a description of the construction
task, and the function interface: its arguments and expected return value.
Model output. A new candidate priority function, written as Python source code.
Execution. The candidate replaces priority in the fixed specification and is run inside the
greedy solver.
Scoring. The solver builds a partition. The fixed evaluator assigns the candidate a numerical
score from that construction.
Feedback. High-scoring candidate programs become examples in later prompts, so subsequent
proposals build on successful rules.
large language model
↓
candidate priority() function
↓
greedy solver builds a partition using it
↓
partition −→numerical score
↓
best-scoring candidates selected for prompts
←
Figure 1: The FunSearch feedback loop.
The return arrow carries selected programs back as
examples for the next model prompt. The task description and function interface remain part of
that prompt.
Feedback carries candidate code selected by its construction score. Thus each rule is evaluated
through a complete construction. Section 4 specifies the fixed solver and the final rule that reaches
195.
4
Our FunSearch Adaptation and the 195 Construction
The implementation uses priority(i,k,partition), solve(n) and evaluate(n). In these code
interfaces, n is the number of classes, k is the next integer to place, and i is a zero-based class
index. The partial partition is a list of n class lists.
3


--- Page 4 ---
The evolved preference.
priority(i,k,partition) returns a numerical preference for plac-
ing k in class i. A higher score makes that class an earlier candidate. The function ranks choices;
it does not decide whether a choice is mathematically allowed.
The fixed construction.
solve(n) starts with n empty classes and considers k = 1, 2, 3, . . .
in order. It computes the priorities, tries classes from highest to lowest score and places k in the
first valid class. Ties are resolved by the smallest index. If every class rejects k, it returns the
partition constructed so far.
The separate function sum_free_addition checks each attempted placement. For an increas-
ing construction, all existing elements of a class S are smaller than k. The only possible new
forbidden sum therefore has k as its largest value: the placement is valid exactly when no distinct
a, b ∈S satisfy a + b = k. The repository checker also tests a + k = b, which cannot occur on this
increasing trajectory.
For example, if a class is {1, 2, 4}, it cannot receive 5 because 1 + 4 = 5. It is rejected even
if the priority ranks it first. The solver then tries the next class. This is the essential division of
responsibility: the priority chooses preferences, while the checker enforces weak sum-freeness.
Listing 1: Pseudocode for solve(n), showing the construction used for the reported result. Internal
guards are omitted.
start with n empty classes
for k = 1, 2, 3, ...:
rank classes by priority(i, k, partition)
try them from highest score to lowest, ties by index
if a class accepts k under the validity check:
place k in the first such class
else:
stop and return the current partition
Since every accepted insertion preserves validity and integers are processed in order, the final
read-only priority builds a partition of an unbroken interval. No earlier placement is revised.
The fixed score.
evaluate(n) counts the entries returned by solve(n). For five classes, only
the baseline count 124 is mapped to zero; the final construction receives score 195.
The final learned priority.
The final rule looks at how far a class currently extends, values
near k/2, additive relationships involving k, values near k, class size and the spread of its elements.
It combines these signals into one numerical preference used to rank the candidate classes; the
separate validity check still controls each placement.
Listing 2 reproduces the signature and
computational body from the saved repository file. NumPy is supplied as np by the specification.
The pair-sum count includes equal summands, so an allowed doubling can affect the prefer-
ence. The coefficients are evolved; their individual effects have not been validated by ablation
experiments.
4


--- Page 5 ---
Listing 2: Verbatim excerpt of fourth_run/WS5_best.py: the signature and computational body
of priority. Only the function’s documentation string is omitted.
def priority(i: int, k: int, partition: list[list]) -> float:
set_max = max(partition[i]) if partition[i] else 0
arr = np.array(partition[i])
window_count = np.sum(np.abs(arr - k/2) <= 2.2)
conflict_penalty = np.sum(np.isin(arr[:, None] + arr, k)) * (k ** 0.48) / 2.9
near_k = np.sum(arr >= k - 9) * np.exp(0.015 * (k - arr.min())) if arr.size > 0 else
0
size_penalty = len(partition[i]) ** 0.33 if len(partition[i]) > 20 else 0
diversity_bonus = np.std(arr) * 0.17 if arr.size > 2 else 0
growth_penalty = -0.078 if set_max > 0.84 * k else 0
return float(set_max) + 2.1 * window_count - 1.95 * conflict_penalty + 0.85 * near_k
- size_penalty + diversity_bonus + growth_penalty
Running the saved rule with solve(5) produces the following classes, where [u, v] denotes
every integer from u to v:
C1 = {1, 2, 4, 8, 11, 22, 25, 53, 63, 68, 139, 149, 154, 177, 182, 195},
C2 = {3, 19, 21, 23} ∪[5, 7] ∪[50, 52] ∪[64, 66]
∪[136, 138] ∪[150, 152] ∪[179, 181] ∪[192, 194],
C3 = {9, 10, 20} ∪[12, 18] ∪[54, 62] ∪[140, 148] ∪[183, 191],
C4 = {24, 153, 178} ∪[26, 49] ∪[155, 176],
C5 = {67} ∪[69, 135].
Their sizes are 16, 25, 37, 49, 68. Independent verification confirms that each integer in [1, 195]
occurs exactly once. Checking all 9,409 pairs a < b with a + b ≤195 finds no monochromatic
triple. The construction establishes
WS(5) ≥195.
Re-executing the final program reproduces this partition. Other saved priorities construct intervals
of lengths 8, 23 and 66 for two, three and four classes, matching the known exact values.
Every class blocks 196: witness pairs are (1, 195), (3, 193), (9, 187), (24, 172) and (67, 129)
in C1, . . . , C5, respectively. This trajectory therefore stops. Extending the displayed partition
requires revising earlier choices, which the fixed greedy solver cannot do. This motivates a global
SAT formulation.
5
SAT Formulation
The greedy constructor commits permanently to each placement.
SAT instead searches for a
complete assignment satisfying all constraints, with the freedom to revise choices when conflicts
arise. A Boolean satisfiability problem consists of true-or-false variables and clauses that must all
hold. A clause is a disjunction: at least one of its alternatives must be true.
For a target interval [1, N], introduce Xv,c for each integer v and colour c ∈{1, . . . , 5}. It
is true exactly when v belongs to class c. The conjunction of the following clauses, written in
conjunctive normal form (CNF), describes the search.
5


--- Page 6 ---
Exactly one class per integer.
Every integer must receive a colour, and two colours cannot
both be selected for the same integer. We express these requirements by
5_
c=1
Xv,c,
(2)
¬Xv,c ∨¬Xv,d
(1 ≤c < d ≤5).
(3)
Here ∨means “or” and ¬ means negation. Together the clauses choose exactly one class for each
v.
Weak Schur constraints.
For each pair a < b with a + b ≤N, its three values cannot all
receive the same colour. For each colour c, add
¬Xa,c ∨¬Xb,c ∨¬Xa+b,c.
(4)
For instance, 2 + 3 = 5 forbids giving 2, 3 and 5 the same colour. Equal summands contribute no
clause. Exactly-one and weak Schur clauses together are equivalent to a valid five-class partition:
a partition satisfies them, and any satisfying assignment decodes into such a partition.
Colour symmetry.
The names of the five classes are arbitrary, so many SAT assignments
describe the same partition and differ only by a permutation of colour labels. Ordering colours by
their first appearance removes this redundant symmetry: colour c may appear only after colour
c −1 has already appeared. For c = 2, . . . , 5 and 1 ≤v ≤N, add
¬Xv,c ∨
v−1
_
u=1
Xu,c−1.
(5)
At v = 1 the disjunction over earlier positions is empty, so only colour 1 is allowed. Any base
partition can be renamed by first appearance, making this a convention on colour names. We use
this convention to implement the increasing-colour information in Rowley’s note (Rowley, 2026),
which refers to the symmetry-breaking methods of Heule (2018).
Structural restrictions.
To focus the search at N = 207, we adopt two restrictions from
Rowley’s note (Rowley, 2026, p. 3 and Fig. 2). These restrictions give partial colour information
while leaving the remaining assignments to the solver.
First, colours repeat with period four within [100, 120]. Integer i and i+4 must have the same
colour whenever both lie in that interval. For 100 ≤i ≤116 and 1 ≤c ≤5, we impose
¬Xi,c ∨Xi+4,c,
¬Xi+4,c ∨Xi,c.
(6)
Second, fourteen colours are fixed to the values in Table 1, taken from the note’s Figure 2. Each
becomes a unit clause Xv,f(v), requiring that colour to be selected.
v
1

3
4
5

16
f(v)

Table 1: The fourteen prescribed colours from Rowley’s structural information.
The structural restrictions select a smaller family of partitions, while retaining every base
requirement. A satisfying assignment therefore still proves a weak Schur lower bound. Failure
within this restricted family would not rule out other weak Schur partitions.

6
The 207 Construction
Structured SAT search produces a verified five-class partition of [1, 207]. This is the
strongest construction obtained in this work and gives
WS(5) ≥207.
It exceeds by eleven the 196 lower bound reported by Eliahou et al. (2012). Table 2 summarizes
the results for the class counts relevant here.

Table 2: Main computational results. FunSearch matches the known values for two, three and
four classes and reaches WS(5) ≥195. Structured SAT establishes WS(5) ≥207, the strongest
construction reported here and eleven above Eliahou et al.’s published lower bound of 196. Dashes
indicate no SAT result reported here.
The final instance and solver.
We set N = 207 and include exactly the constraints of Sec-
tion 5: one class per integer, no distinct-summand monochromatic sum, first-appearance colour
ordering, period four within [100, 120], and the fourteen prescribed colours. The latter two restric-
tions are the partial structural information taken from Rowley’s note. Table 3 gives the resulting
clause counts.
Clause family
Count
At least one colour
207
At most one colour
2,070
Weak Schur constraints
53,045
First-appearance ordering
828

170
Fixed colours
14
Total
56,334
Table 3: The final SAT instance: 1,035 variables and 56,334 clauses.
There are 10,609 pairs a < b with a + b ≤207, each yielding five weak Schur clauses. The
generator numbers Xv,c by 5(v −1)+c and writes the complete formula in DIMACS CNF format,
including the fourteen fixed colours as unit clauses.
SLIME5 (Riveros, 2020), run on this file with default settings, returns a satisfying assignment.
In the recorded experiment, it found the assignment in approximately 107 seconds. Reading each
integer’s selected colour gives the five classes.
The certificate.
The complete construction is supplied in the machine-readable 207 certificate.
Its five lists allow the result to be checked without repeating the search. Table 4 compares their
sizes with those of the FunSearch construction.

Independent verification.
The certificate can be checked independently by confirming that
the five classes cover [1, 207] exactly, with no repeated or missing integers, and contain no forbidden
weak Schur triple. Verification examines all 10,609 pairs a < b with a+b ≤207 and confirms that
a, b and a + b never share a colour. Thus the five lists form a partition of the required interval
into weakly sum-free classes.
Proposition 1 The certificate partitions [1, 207] into five weakly sum-free classes.
Hence
WS(5) ≥207.
Proof.
Exact interval coverage establishes a partition of [1, 207].
The exhaustive pair check
establishes (1) in every class. These are the defining requirements of a weak Schur partition, so
this certificate proves the lower bound.
The check is independent of the SAT solver and generator. The public verifier equivalently
checks distinct pairs within each class and tests whether their sum is absent from that class.
The SAT assignment yields the same partition as the certificate and satisfies all 56,334 clauses.
The mathematical lower bound follows directly from exact interval coverage and weak sum-
freeness.
Rowley’s source also gives a partition at 207. Our returned certificate differs from its Figure 3
even after renaming colours: the greatest agreement over all 5! colour permutations is 191 of the
207 positions.
7
Discussion and Conclusion
FunSearch searches for a heuristic program used inside a fixed greedy construction. The learned
priority ranks candidate classes, while a separate validity check enforces weak sum-freeness. This
method constructs a verified partition establishing WS(5) ≥195, but cannot revise earlier choices
when the next insertion is blocked.
The SAT formulation performs global constraint search,
allowing assignments to be reconsidered while enforcing the full set of requirements, and reaches
WS(5) ≥207.
The difference illustrates the importance of search architecture. The gap from 195 to 207
concerns the particular greedy constructor and learned rule used here; it does not prove a general
limitation of FunSearch. A natural future direction is a hybrid approach in which learned heuristics
guide an exact solver that can revise assignments and enforce global constraints.
Both results are explicit, independently verified lower bounds, rather than a determination of
the exact value of WS(5). The principal result of this paper is the structured SAT construction
establishing WS(5) ≥207.
Code and data availability.
The commit-stable repository snapshot contains the saved pri-
ority and specification, plus the linked 207 certificate and verifier. The supplement supplies both
certificates, the CNF generator and instance, signed solver output, independent checks and soft-
ware metadata. Verification uses only Python; re-executing the final 195 program also requires
NumPy.
8


--- Page 9 ---
The final constructions can be checked from these artifacts. The original winning FunSearch
run’s exact model, seed and search configuration are not completely preserved, so the whole
evolutionary discovery process cannot be reconstructed from them.
